Reference: Balcer and Lippman (1984)

Model Setting

The paper studies the demand for innovations: a firm that uses a technology which outside research improves from time to time must decide, each period, whether to pay a switching cost and adopt the best available technology now or to postpone adoption. The question is the one raised by Schumpeter, that a new machine is a link in a chain of improvements and the firm must decide at which link to act, and by Rosenberg (1976), that the timing of adoption is governed by technological expectations. The supply of innovations is exogenous: discoveries arrive from a research process that does not respond to the buyer or to other agents. Two features distinguish the model from earlier adoption models with a single anticipated innovation (Kamien and Schwartz 1972): the firm anticipates a sequence of innovations of random size, and the time between innovations has an arbitrary distribution, so that the firm revises its forecast of the next discovery as time passes without one.

The firm's problem is a discounted dynamic programme whose state is the technological lag, the discovery potential and the time since the last discovery. Theorem 1 shows that the optimal policy is a threshold rule: adopt the current best practice if and only if the lag exceeds a critical number that depends on the discovery potential and on the elapsed time. Lemma 1 shows that the threshold rises with the fixed cost. Theorem 2 shows that the threshold moves with elapsed time in the same direction as the hazard rate of the next discovery; under a decreasing hazard rate a technology that was rejected when it appeared is adopted later, with no new information except the absence of discoveries. Theorem 3 shows that a faster pace of innovation and larger innovations raise the threshold, so that expectations of rapid progress delay adoption. Two worked examples show that uncertainty about the size of innovations can hasten adoption, and that a faster pace gives less frequent, larger adoptions and a worse installed technology in the short run. The paper contains no estimation and no numerical calibration; all results are analytical.

Technological Process

The probabilistic evolution of technology is summarized by three variables: the state of technological knowledge yyy, the discovery potential iii, and the time nnn since the last discovery. The scalar yyy is the best implementable technology, for instance an index that lowers a constant marginal cost. The integer iii embodies the history of the process up to the last discovery and signals the pace and the size of the next innovation. Time is discrete. The discovery potential follows a semi-Markov process with embedded one-step transition matrix P=(Pij)P=(P_{ij})P=(Pij​), where PijP_{ij}Pij​ is the probability that the next level is jjj given the current level iii, and Pii>0P_{ii}>0Pii​>0 is allowed. The holding time TiT_iTi​, the random number of periods until the next innovation when the potential is iii, is a positive integer with distribution function GiG_iGi​ and need not be memoryless. At the instant of an innovation the potential moves from iii to jjj and yyy rises by a nonnegative amount ZiZ_iZi​ with distribution function FiF_iFi​ and mean μi\mu_iμi​; the realized size is observed immediately, and Fi(0)>0F_i(0)>0Fi​(0)>0 is allowed, so a discovery may change only the potential. Given iii, the next potential JJJ, the size ZiZ_iZi​ and the event of a discovery next period are mutually independent, and the evolution after the discovery depends only on the new pair of knowledge and potential. Because elapsed time carries information only through the fact that no discovery has occurred, the updated distribution of the time to discovery is the truncation of GiG_iGi​. The conditional probability of a discovery next period, given potential iii and nnn periods without discovery, is:

Threshold Policy

Theorem 1 (existence) states that there are critical numbers ξi(n)\xi_i(n)ξi​(n) such that, when the discovery potential is iii and nnn periods have elapsed since the last innovation, the firm adopts the best available technology if and only if z≥ξi(n)z\geq\xi_i(n)z≥ξi​(n). The proof compares the two arguments of the maximum in the rewritten functional equation. The function hhh is zero at z=0z=0z=0 and increasing in zzz. An extra unit of lag can never be worth more than Δ\DeltaΔ, that is V(j,u+z,n)−V(j,u,n)≤ΔzV(j,u+z,n)-V(j,u,n)\leq\Delta zV(j,u+z,n)−V(j,u,n)≤Δz, and when it is carried forward it is cashed in at least one period later, so:

Time Since the Last Innovation

Can the firm adopt a technology it previously declined, when in the meantime no discovery was made and the discovery potential did not change? Under perfect foresight the answer is no: the firm buys a new technology as soon as it becomes available or not at all. Theorem 2 gives the answer under uncertainty: for given iii, if TiT_iTi​ has a nondecreasing hazard rate then ξi(n)\xi_i(n)ξi​(n) is a nondecreasing function of nnn, and if TiT_iTi​ has a nonincreasing hazard rate then ξi(n)\xi_i(n)ξi​(n) is a nonincreasing function of nnn; the monotonicity is strict when the hazard rate is strictly monotone. When pi(n)p_i(n)pi​(n) increases in nnn the industry becomes ripe for a new discovery, and a technology not worth installing today is worth even less tomorrow, so any adoption takes place at the moment of a discovery. When pi(n)p_i(n)pi​(n) decreases in nnn, the lack of success signals that further advances are less likely, the option value of waiting shrinks, and the extant technology is eventually installed once the falling threshold reaches the unchanged lag. A corollary noted by the authors is that a monopolistic supplier of innovations can force adoption of its current technology by shutting down its research and development.

The proof truncates TiT_iTi​ at an integer kkk and lets kkk grow. Write q(n)q(n)q(n) for the truncated hazard rate and suppress iii and kkk, so that V(z,n)V(z,n)V(z,n), ξ(n)\xi(n)ξ(n), h(z,n)h(z,n)h(z,n) and EV(U+z,0)EV(U+z,0)EV(U+z,0) denote the truncated objects. In the nondecreasing case q(k)=1q(k)=1q(k)=1, and a backward induction on nnn establishes:

∂h(z,n)∂z≤∂h(z,n+1)∂zwhenever z<min⁡{ξ(n),ξ(n−1)}(15)\frac{\partial h(z,n)}{\partial z}\leq\frac{\partial h(z,n+1)}{\partial z}\qquad\text{whenever }z<\min\left\{\xi(n),\xi(n-1)\right\} \tag{15}∂z∂h(z,n)​≤∂z∂h(z,n+1)​whenever z<min{ξ(n),ξ(n−1)}(15)

Since h(0,n)=0h(0,n)=0h(0,n)=0 for every nnn, a steeper hhh is a higher hhh, and a higher waiting curve crosses the adoption line further to the right, which gives ξ(n)≥ξ(n−1)\xi(n)\geq\xi(n-1)ξ(n)≥ξ(n−1). The slope ranking holds because a marginal unit of lag is worth more when it will be bundled with an imminent discovery, at no extra fixed cost, than when it must be carried through further periods of discounting. In the nonincreasing case the truncation sets q(k)=0q(k)=0q(k)=0, so that no discovery ever occurs once k−1k-1k−1 periods have elapsed. The waiting curve then reduces to:

and ξ(n)=K/Δ\xi(n)=K/\Deltaξ(n)=K/Δ for n≥k−1n\geq k-1n≥k−1: with nothing left to wait for, the firm adopts whenever adoption breaks even. The induction then steps backwards. For a lag between ξ(n+2)\xi(n+2)ξ(n+2) and ξ(n+1)\xi(n+1)ξ(n+1) the value V(z,n)V(z,n)V(z,n) is written out two periods ahead as the larger of an adopt-now term and a wait-one-period term, and evaluated at z=ξ(n+1)z=\xi(n+1)z=ξ(n+1), where by the definition of the threshold:

Pace of Innovation

To compare thresholds across levels of the discovery potential, the levels are labelled so that a higher level means larger and sooner innovations. Innovation sizes are stochastically increasing in iii:

Fi(z)≥Fi+1(z)for all z, i=0,±1,±2,…(18)F_i(z)\geq F_{i+1}(z)\qquad\text{for all }z,\ i=0,\pm1,\pm2,\ldots \tag{18}Fi​(z)≥Fi+1​(z)for all z, i=0,±1,±2,…(18)

The potential reached after the next innovation is stochastically increasing in the current potential:

∑j=k∞Pij is nondecreasing in i for each fixed k(19)\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}P_{ij}\ \text{is nondecreasing in }i\text{ for each fixed }k \tag{19}j=k∑∞​Pij​ is nondecreasing in i for each fixed k(19)

This does not make the potential nondecreasing over time, which would require Pij=0P_{ij}=0Pij​=0 for all j<ij<ij<i. The time to the next innovation is shorter at a higher potential. A natural formalization is that TiT_iTi​ is stochastically larger than Ti+1T_{i+1}Ti+1​, which the authors suspect is sufficient at n=0n=0n=0, but the theorem uses the stronger ordering of hazard rates; the two conditions are, in turn:

Gi(n)≤Gi+1(n)for all n≥0,pi(n)≤pi+1(n)for n≥0(20)G_i(n)\leq G_{i+1}(n)\quad\text{for all }n\geq0,\qquad p_i(n)\leq p_{i+1}(n)\quad\text{for }n\geq0 \tag{20}Gi​(n)≤Gi+1​(n)for all n≥0,pi​(n)≤pi+1​(n)for n≥0(20)

When the hazard rate is nondecreasing in nnn, the stochastic ordering, and with it the hazard ordering, can be replaced by a weaker ordering of the expected discount factor to the next discovery (which the paper calls the expected discounted time until the next discovery):

Theorem 3 has two parts. If the process satisfies the size ordering, the transition ordering and the hazard ordering, and either TiT_iTi​ is not a function of iii or Pij=0P_{ij}=0Pij​=0 for j<i−1j<i-1j<i−1, then ξi(n)≤ξi+1(n)\xi_i(n)\leq\xi_{i+1}(n)ξi​(n)≤ξi+1​(n) for all iii and nnn. If the process satisfies the size ordering, the transition ordering and Di≤Di+1D_i\leq D_{i+1}Di​≤Di+1​, and the hazard rate is nondecreasing for each iii, then ξi(0)≤ξi+1(0)\xi_i(0)\leq\xi_{i+1}(0)ξi​(0)≤ξi+1​(0) for all iii. The minimum lag at which the firm adopts therefore rises with the pace of technological progress: in a rapidly changing environment the firm avoids locking itself in. The restriction Pij=0P_{ij}=0Pij​=0 for j<i−1j<i-1j<i−1 lets the pace slow down, but by no more than one level at a time.

The proof works with the value iteration on the number mmm of transitions remaining:

Vm+1(i,z,n)=max⁡{−K+Δz; hm(i,z,n+1)}+Hm(i,n+1)(22)V_{m+1}(i,z,n)=\max\left\{-K+\Delta z;\ h_m(i,z,n+1)\right\}+H_m(i,n+1) \tag{22}Vm+1​(i,z,n)=max{−K+Δz; hm​(i,z,n+1)}+Hm​(i,n+1)(22)

with V0≡0V_0\equiv0V0​≡0 and with HmH_mHm​ and hmh_mhm​ defined as HHH and hhh with VmV_mVm​ in place of VVV. Each VmV_mVm​ is convex in zzz, because a maximum of convex functions and a nonnegative mixture of convex functions are convex. Convexity makes the marginal value of lag nondecreasing in zzz, so a stochastically larger innovation raises the expected marginal value of the lag the firm already carries; by induction ∂Vm(i,z,n)/∂z\partial V_m(i,z,n)/\partial z∂Vm​(i,z,n)/∂z is nondecreasing in iii, and the transition ordering then makes the post-discovery marginal value nondecreasing in iii. Short Run and Long Run

Theorem 3 does not imply that the firm's installed technology is better at every date when the pace is faster. The paper's deterministic example has two levels of discovery potential that never change, slow (i=0i=0i=0) and fast (i=1i=1i=1), with Zi≡x>0Z_i\equiv x>0Zi​≡x>0, Pii=1P_{ii}=1Pii​=1, T0≡mT_0\equiv mT0​≡m and T1≡m−1>0T_1\equiv m-1>0T1​≡m−1>0 (here xxx is the common size of an innovation and mmm an integer). The costs and the discount factor satisfy:

−K−sx+x1−β(1−βm)=0(24)-K-sx+\frac{x}{1-\beta}\left(1-\beta^m\right)=0 \tag{24}−K−sx+1−βx​(1−βm)=0(24)

Ci(j)=[−K−jsx+jx1−β]βjTi1−βjTi(25)C_i(j)=\left[-K-jsx+\frac{jx}{1-\beta}\right]\frac{\beta^{jT_i}}{1-\beta^{jT_i}} \tag{25}Ci​(j)=[−K−jsx+1−βjx​]1−βjTi​βjTi​​(25)

Under the parameter restriction, C0(1)≥C0(j)C_0(1)\geq C_0(j)C0​(1)≥C0​(j) for every jjj, so at the slow pace the firm adopts every discovery. At the fast pace, with δ=βT1\delta=\beta^{T_1}δ=βT1​:

C1(1)−C1(2)=δ2(sx−x)1−δ2(26)C_1(1)-C_1(2)=\frac{\delta^2\left(sx-x\right)}{1-\delta^2} \tag{26}C1​(1)−C1​(2)=1−δ2δ2(sx−x)​(26)

The paper prints this difference without the factor δ2\delta^2δ2 and writes the bracket as sx−(1−β)x/(1−β)sx-(1-\beta)x/(1-\beta)sx−(1−β)x/(1−β); the sign is the same. Hence C1(1)<C1(2)C_1(1)<C_1(2)C1​(1)<C1​(2) if sss is sufficiently small, the firm adopts every second discovery at the fast pace, and ξ1(n)>ξ0(n)\xi_1(n)>\xi_0(n)ξ1​(n)>ξ0​(n). The slow-pace firm then has the better installed technology at times m,m+1,…,2m−3m,m+1,\ldots,2m-3m,m+1,…,2m−3 and 3m,3m+1,…,4m−53m,3m+1,\ldots,4m-53m,3m+1,…,4m−5, while from time 2(m−1)22(m-1)^22(m−1)2 onward the fast-pace firm is always ahead. A faster pace therefore produces larger but less frequent adoptions, a higher efficiency of installed equipment in the long run, and not necessarily in the short run, in line with Rosenberg's observation that rapid technological progress need not mean rapid introduction of innovations.

Announcements

Theorems 2 and 3 together explain why the mere announcement of a forthcoming technology delays purchases of the current one. In the model an announcement is a discovery of size zero that raises the discovery potential. Take a state (i,z,n)(i,z,n)(i,z,n) with K/Δ<z<ξi(n)K/\Delta<z<\xi_i(n)K/Δ<z<ξi​(n) and a decreasing hazard rate, and suppose there is a finite τ\tauτ with z=ξi(n+τ)z=\xi_i(n+\tau)z=ξi​(n+τ), so that absent news the firm would adopt at time n+τn+\taun+τ. Let a discovery of size zero occur at a time Θ\ThetaΘ with n<Θ<τ+nn<\Theta<\tau+nn<Θ<τ+n and move the potential from iii to j≥ij\geq ij≥i, with no further discovery in the next n+τ−Θn+\tau-\Thetan+τ−Θ periods. Then:

ξj(0)>ξj(n+τ)≥ξi(n+τ)(27)\xi_j(0)>\xi_j(n+\tau)\geq\xi_i(n+\tau) \tag{27}ξj​(0)>ξj​(n+τ)≥ξi​(n+τ)(27)

The lag is unchanged, but the announcement restarts the clock and raises the potential, so at the scheduled date the required lag is ξj(n+τ−Θ)\xi_j(n+\tau-\Theta)ξj​(n+τ−Θ) instead of ξi(n+τ)\xi_i(n+\tau)ξi​(n+τ) and adoption is delayed beyond n+τn+\taun+τ. The authors read the 1964 announcement by IBM of its not yet existing model 360/91, just before Control Data delivered its model 6600, in this way: the announcement raised buyers' thresholds, and the rival had to cut its price.

Hazard-Rate Examples and Inside Information

Two specifications of the discovery process deliver the two cases of Theorem 2. In both, the public information is the state of knowledge, the discovery potential, the elapsed time and the hazard rate. In Example 1 a discovery requires two steps, basic research followed by engineering implementation, whose completion times are independent geometric random variables with parameters pip_ipi​ and qiq_iqi​ (the symbol pip_ipi​ without an argument is the first-step parameter, not the hazard rate). The hazard rate of their sum is:

pi(n)=piqi−piqi[(1−pi)/(1−qi)]n−1pi−qi[(1−pi)/(1−qi)]n−1,n≥1(28)p_i(n)=\frac{p_iq_i-p_iq_i\left[(1-p_i)/(1-q_i)\right]^{n-1}}{p_i-q_i\left[(1-p_i)/(1-q_i)\right]^{n-1}},\qquad n\geq1 \tag{28}pi​(n)=pi​−qi​[(1−pi​)/(1−qi​)]n−1pi​qi​−pi​qi​[(1−pi​)/(1−qi​)]n−1​,n≥1(28)

It increases in nnn, starting from piqip_iq_ipi​qi​ at n=2n=2n=2; the paper gives the limit as qiq_iqi​, which is the limit of the expression when pi>qip_i>q_ipi​>qi​. As time passes it becomes more likely that the first step has been completed, so by Theorem 2 a technology that was not worth buying when it appeared is worth even less later. Inside information here is knowledge of whether the first step is complete. Let pi(n+m;n)p_i(n+m;n)pi​(n+m;n) be the hazard rate at time n+mn+mn+m given inside information at time nnn; it equals qi>pi(n+m)q_i>p_i(n+m)qi​>pi​(n+m) if the first step is complete and pi(m)<pi(n+m)p_i(m)<p_i(n+m)pi​(m)<pi​(n+m) if it is not. The authors conclude that such information is worthless to the buyer, because a technology worth adopting is adopted at the moment it is discovered.

In Example 2 the time to discovery is geometric with an unknown parameter, equal to λ\lambdaλ with probability qiq_iqi​ and to λ′\lambda'λ′ with probability 1−qi1-q_i1−qi​, where λ>λ′\lambda>\lambda'λ>λ′. The hazard rate is:

pi(n)=qiλ(1−λ)n−1+(1−qi)λ′(1−λ′)n−1qi(1−λ)n−1+(1−qi)(1−λ′)n−1,n≥1(29)p_i(n)=\frac{q_i\lambda(1-\lambda)^{n-1}+(1-q_i)\lambda'(1-\lambda')^{n-1}}{q_i(1-\lambda)^{n-1}+(1-q_i)(1-\lambda')^{n-1}},\qquad n\geq1 \tag{29}pi​(n)=qi​(1−λ)n−1+(1−qi​)(1−λ′)n−1qi​λ(1−λ)n−1+(1−qi​)λ′(1−λ′)n−1​,n≥1(29)

It decreases from qiλ+(1−qi)λ′q_i\lambda+(1-q_i)\lambda'qi​λ+(1−qi​)λ′ to λ′\lambda'λ′ as nnn goes from one to infinity, because the posterior probability of the low parameter rises from 1−qi1-q_i1−qi​ to one: research that has not yet succeeded is probably on an unpromising path. By Theorem 2 the threshold falls with elapsed time, and a technology that did not look good enough while the future looked promising is adopted once the future looks dimmer. Inside information, knowledge of which parameter is the true one, is valuable in both directions: a buyer about to purchase on the public hazard rate may postpone on learning that prospects are good, and a buyer about to postpone may purchase on learning that they are bad.

Scope

The paper characterizes the decision rule of a single buyer. It does not derive the distribution of the adoption date, a diffusion curve across firms, or comparative statics in market size or in the discount factor, and it keeps the supply of innovations exogenous. The authors point to the joining of the two sides of the market as the main open question: by Theorem 3, more research effort by suppliers raises buyers' expectations and hence their adoption thresholds, and a large buyer whose expectations rise with suppliers' success can push suppliers toward an ever faster pace of innovation. They also note that innovations are reduced to a one-dimensional cost reduction, leaving out uncertainty about the profitability of a new discovery, minor adjustments to existing equipment, learning by doing and compatibility between innovations.

Without the fixed charge the problem would be trivial: with K=0K=0K=0 and Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0 the firm would set xm=Ymx_m=Y_mxm​=Ym​ in every period. The charge KKK is paid per switch and not per unit, so two innovations adopted together cost one KKK instead of two. This economy of scale in adoption is the only reason to skip or postpone, and it is weighed against the profit lost while the lag is carried. Since the objective is linear in the levels and the costs depend on differences only, the problem can be restated in terms of the lag z=y−xz=y-xz=y−x, which is done in equations (5) and (6).

This is an assumption on primitives, equation (9) of the paper: first-order stochastic dominance of innovation sizes across levels of the discovery potential. Fi(z)F_i(z)Fi​(z) is the probability that the next innovation at potential iii is no larger than zzz; a smaller distribution function at every zzz means more mass on large sizes. So Zi+1Z_{i+1}Zi+1​ is stochastically larger than ZiZ_iZi​, and for every nondecreasing function ggg,

∫0∞g(u) dFi+1(u)≥∫0∞g(u) dFi(u)\int_0^{\infty}g(u)\,dF_{i+1}(u)\geq\int_0^{\infty}g(u)\,dF_i(u)∫0∞​g(u)dFi+1​(u)≥∫0∞​g(u)dFi​(u)

In particular μi+1≥μi\mu_{i+1}\geq\mu_iμi+1​≥μi​. The index iii runs over all integers, and the labelling is a normalization: levels are ordered so that a higher level is better.

The assumption is used in the proof of Theorem 3 through the convexity of VmV_mVm​ in the lag (equation (22)). Convexity makes the marginal value ∂Vm(j,u+z,n)/∂z\partial V_m(j,u+z,n)/\partial z∂Vm​(j,u+z,n)/∂z nondecreasing in uuu, so taking ggg to be this marginal value shows that the expected marginal value of the lag already carried is larger when the coming innovation is stochastically larger: a bigger innovation makes it more likely that the old lag will be cashed in together with it. That raises the slope of the waiting curve hhh in equation (10) and, with it, the threshold. The assumption orders whole distributions; an ordering of means alone would not suffice, because ggg is not linear.

This is the second ordering assumption, equation (10) of the paper. The sum ∑j≥kPij\sum_{j\geq k}P_{ij}∑j≥k​Pij​ is the probability that the potential after the next discovery is at least kkk, starting from iii. Requiring it to be nondecreasing in iii for every kkk says that row i+1i+1i+1 of the transition matrix first-order stochastically dominates row iii: a higher current potential leads to a stochastically higher next potential. Equivalently, for every nondecreasing sequence gjg_jgj​,

∑jPi+1,j gj≥∑jPij gj\sum_jP_{i+1,j}\,g_j\geq\sum_jP_{ij}\,g_jj∑​Pi+1,j​gj​≥j∑​Pij​gj​

The condition is a persistence property and not a monotonicity property of the path. It does not say that the potential rises over time; that would require Pij=0P_{ij}=0Pij​=0 for all j<ij<ij<i. A symmetric random walk on the integers satisfies it, although the potential falls half of the time.

In the proof of Theorem 3 the sequence gjg_jgj​ is the expected marginal value of lag after a discovery that leads to potential jjj, which the induction hypothesis makes nondecreasing in jjj. The assumption then transfers monotonicity from the next potential to the current one, so that the discovery branch of hmh_mhm​ in equation (22) has a slope that is nondecreasing in iii. Together with equation (18) it also gives the long-run meaning of a higher potential: from a higher starting level, all future potentials, and hence all future sizes, are stochastically higher.

These are two alternative ways to say that the next innovation comes sooner at a higher potential, equations (11b) and (11c) of the paper. The first is the usual stochastic order: Gi(n)=P(Ti≤n)G_i(n)=P(T_i\leq n)Gi​(n)=P(Ti​≤n) is smaller at iii than at i+1i+1i+1, so TiT_iTi​ is stochastically larger than Ti+1T_{i+1}Ti+1​. The second orders the hazard rates of equation (1) period by period: after any number of quiet periods, a discovery is at least as likely at the higher potential.

The hazard ordering is the stronger one. By the product formula in the derivation of equation (1),

1−Gi(n)=∏l=1n(1−pi(l))≥∏l=1n(1−pi+1(l))=1−Gi+1(n)1-G_i(n)=\prod_{l=1}^{n}\left(1-p_i(l)\right)\geq\prod_{l=1}^{n}\left(1-p_{i+1}(l)\right)=1-G_{i+1}(n)1−Gi​(n)=l=1∏n​(1−pi​(l))≥l=1∏n​(1−pi+1​(l))=1−Gi+1​(n)

so the second condition implies the first, and the converse fails in general. The authors conjecture that the first condition, with equations (18) and (19), is enough for ξi(0)≤ξi+1(0)\xi_i(0)\leq\xi_{i+1}(0)ξi​(0)≤ξi+1​(0), but the first part of Theorem 3 is proved under the second.

The reason is that the threshold ξi(n)\xi_i(n)ξi​(n) is compared at every elapsed time nnn, and after nnn quiet periods what matters is the conditional distribution of the remaining wait; the hazard ordering is preserved by this conditioning and the plain stochastic order is not. In the proof, a higher hazard moves weight in hmh_mhm​ from the no-discovery branch to the discovery branch, and the side condition of Theorem 3 (either TiT_iTi​ does not depend on iii, or Pij=0P_{ij}=0Pij​=0 for j<i−1j<i-1j<i−1) ensures that this raises the slope.

Di=EβTi=∑n≥1βn[Gi(n)−Gi(n−1)]D_i=E\beta^{T_i}=\sum_{n\geq1}\beta^n\left[G_i(n)-G_i(n-1)\right]Di​=EβTi​=∑n≥1​βn[Gi​(n)−Gi​(n−1)] is the expected present value of one unit paid at the date of the next discovery. It lies between zero and β\betaβ and is larger when the discovery tends to come sooner. The paper calls it the expected discounted time until the next discovery; it is a discount factor and not a time.

The condition Di≤Di+1D_i\leq D_{i+1}Di​≤Di+1​ is equation (12) of the paper, and the paper introduces it as a weakening of the stochastic order in equation (20). Indeed βt\beta^tβt is decreasing in ttt, so if TiT_iTi​ is stochastically larger than Ti+1T_{i+1}Ti+1​ then

The paper describes mmm as the number of transitions or decision epochs remaining: after the last one nothing changes and no further decision is made. Two things make the iteration useful. Second, each property can be proved by induction on mmm, because the map preserves it: a maximum of convex functions is convex and a mixture of convex functions is convex, so Vm+1V_{m+1}Vm+1​ is convex in zzz if VmV_mVm​ is. Convexity means that the marginal value of lag is nondecreasing in the lag, which is what links the orderings in equations (18) to (21) to the slope of hmh_mhm​, and the slope of hmh_mhm​ to the threshold through equation (12).

This is the parameter restriction of the two-pace example in footnote 25 of the paper, marked there with an asterisk. It ties the fixed cost KKK to the size xxx of an innovation, the unit cost sss, the discount factor and the slow holding time mmm. Two equivalent readings are useful. Since 1−βm=(1−β)(1+β+⋯+βm−1)1-\beta^m=(1-\beta)\left(1+\beta+\cdots+\beta^{m-1}\right)1−βm=(1−β)(1+β+⋯+βm−1),

The restriction is a knife-edge chosen to make the algebra short. It is used in the derivations of equations (25) and (26) to eliminate KKK. At the slow pace it makes adopting every discovery optimal. At the fast pace the cycle lasts only m−1m-1m−1 periods, one innovation no longer pays for itself within a cycle, and bundling two innovations under one fixed charge becomes attractive when sss is small.
